plain: Social media gives companies real-time insight into customer sentiment, preferences, and behavior, which helps them make faster and more informed decisions on products, marketing, and customer service. By tracking what people say and how they engage, businesses can spot trends early, test messaging, and respond to problems before they escalate. Four useful pieces of social media data are: 1) brand mentions (how often and where people talk about the company), 2) the number of retweets or shares (how far a message spreads), 3) sentiment of comments (positive, negative, or neutral reactions), and 4) follower growth rate (how quickly an audience is expanding). Together, these metrics reveal both what customers think and how effectively content is reaching them.

plain: Fanny packs deserve more credit as a practical accessory for walking around town. Unlike a backpack, a fanny pack sits at your front or side, so you can see it and access it without taking it off, which also makes it harder for pickpockets to reach. They're lightweight, don't cause shoulder or back strain the way a heavy bag can, and modern designs come in enough styles that they no longer look purely functional. Its official name is technically 'the State of Rhode Island,' shortened from a longer historical title. It fits entirely within a roughly 48-mile stretch, making it small enough to drive across in under an hour.

plain: The Battle of Hastings, fought on October 14, 1066, was between the Norman army led by William, Duke of Normandy (later known as William the Conqueror), and the English army led by King Harold II (Harold Godwinson). William's forces included cavalry, archers, and infantry, while Harold's army was largely composed of infantry, including his elite housecarls, who had just marched south after defeating a Norwegian invasion at Stamford Bridge. William's victory, aided by Harold's death during the battle, allowed him to claim the English throne, beginning Norman rule over England.

Electric-types like Pikachu, Raichu, Jolteon, or Zapdos can hit water types for double damage without taking extra damage back, since Electric isn't resisted by most Water types' secondary typing. Grass-types like Venusaur, Sceptile, or Ferrothorn also deal double damage, though be careful if the opposing Pokémon has a secondary Flying or Poison typing, which can reduce Grass's effectiveness. A strong pick would be an Electric-type with high speed, like Jolteon, since it can often outspeed and knock out a Water-type before it attacks.

plain: Avocados are incredibly versatile and can be used in both savory and sweet dishes. The most obvious is guacamole, mashed with lime, onion, cilantro, and chili. They're also great sliced onto toast with salt, chili flakes, and a fried egg, or added to salads for creaminess. In Mexican cuisine, they top tacos, burritos, and tortas. Sushi rolls like the California roll often include avocado for texture. They can be blended into smoothies or even chocolate mousse, since their fat content creates a rich, creamy texture without dairy. Avocado can also be used in pasta sauces, as a mayo substitute in sandwiches, or baked into brownies for added moisture.

plain: One of the most highly regarded books on the Battle of Stalingrad is 'Stalingrad' by Antony Beevor, published in 1998. It's praised for combining rigorous archival research, including newly opened Soviet records, with vivid, readable narrative that captures the human cost of the battle from both German and Soviet perspectives. Another strong option is 'Enemy at the Gates' by William Craig, which focuses more on individual stories and the sniper duels that became legendary. For a more analytical, military-strategy focused account, 'Stalingrad' by David Glantz offers deep operational detail. If you want one accessible, well-researched book to start with, Beevor's is generally the top recommendation.

plain: Hinduism is often considered the oldest major world religion still practiced today, with roots tracing back over 4,000 years to the Indus Valley Civilization and the Vedic period in ancient India, around 1500 BCE for its earliest texts (the Vedas). Unlike many religions, it doesn't have a single founder and developed gradually from a blend of Indo-Aryan and indigenous South Asian traditions. Some scholars also point to animistic and shamanistic practices, or ancient religions like those of ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia, as older forms of organized belief, though most of those aren't practiced in continuous form today. So while exact 'oldest' claims depend on definition, Hinduism is the most commonly cited answer for a living, continuously practiced religion.

plain: As of the mid-2020s, Voyager 1 is over 15 billion miles (about 24 billion kilometers) from Earth, making it the most distant human-made object in space. It's traveling through interstellar space, having crossed the heliopause (the boundary of the Sun's influence) in 2012, and is currently moving through the constellation Ophiuchus as seen from Earth. It travels at roughly 38,000 miles per hour and takes over 22 hours for a radio signal to reach it one way. Because it's constantly moving outward, its exact distance changes daily; NASA's Voyager mission website publishes a real-time distance tracker if you want the current figure.

plain: Colleges typically evaluate applicants using a combination of factors. Academic performance is central: GPA, course rigor (like AP or IB classes), and standardized test scores where required. Beyond grades, admissions officers look at extracurricular involvement, leadership roles, and depth of commitment to activities rather than just quantity. Essays and personal statements matter a lot, since they reveal writing ability, self-reflection, and personality. Letters of recommendation from teachers or counselors provide outside perspective. Many schools also consider demonstrated interest, interviews, and how a student's background or experiences would contribute to campus diversity. Some colleges weigh legacy status, athletic recruitment, or first-generation status as well, depending on their specific priorities.

plain: There are several distinct snowboarding disciplines. Freestyle involves tricks and jumps performed in terrain parks, on rails, boxes, and jumps, or in halfpipes. Freeride is about riding natural, ungroomed terrain like backcountry powder, focusing on style and line choice rather than tricks. Alpine (or carving) uses a stiffer, narrower board and hard boots for high-speed, precise turns on groomed slopes, similar to ski racing. Slopestyle combines rails, jumps, and other features in a judged course, common in competitions like the X Games and Olympics. Big air focuses on a single large jump, judged on height, trick difficulty, and execution. Boardercross is a timed race where multiple riders navigate a course with jumps and banked turns simultaneously.
